WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Congress passed a $300 billion farm bill over President Bush's veto for a second time Wednesday, a step made necessary by a clerical error when the original bill passed. Congress overrode President Bush's second veto of a $300 billion farm bill. The Senate voted 80-14 to approve the measure over Bush's objections, following a 317-109 vote in the House of Representatives. Both votes were well above the two-thirds majority needed to override the veto, which Bush delivered Wednesday morning. Congress overrode an earlier veto of the farm bill last month, even though lawmakers had discovered that 34 pages were missing in the version originally sent to the White House. In spiking the latest version, Bush said he objected to its continued subsidies for the wealthy and its use of budget gimmicks to hide a $20 billion increase in spending. But Sen. Kent Conrad, the chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, said the measure actually saves the government $110 million. "This bill does not add to the deficit or debt, because this bill is paid for," he said. "That is not my claim. That is the finding of the Congressional Budget Office." The discovery of the missing section, Title III, prompted concerns from House Republicans that the override vote was improper. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said the sections of the bill that were originally sent to the president had become law after Congress voted to override Bush's first veto. But to put Title III into effect, Congress re-passed the entire legislation, including the missing pages, and resent it to Bush. The House voted 306-110 at the end of May. The Senate voted 77-15 for the bill at the beginning of June. Two-thirds of the $300 billion in spending for the farm bill will go for nutrition programs such as food stamps. Another $40 billion will go toward farm subsidies, and $30 billion is allocated for payments to farms to keep land idle and other environmental programs. After vetoing the latest version of the farm bill, Bush scolded Congress on Wednesday for not "modifying certain objectionable, onerous and fiscally imprudent provisions. ... I am returning this bill for the same reasons as stated in my veto message." When he vetoed the first version of the farm bill, Bush said it "continues subsidies for the wealthy and increases farm bill spending by more than $20 billion, while using budget gimmicks to hide much of the increase." The president said it would hurt efforts to improve American farmers' access to overseas markets. Congress has passed one other bill over Bush's objections: legislation for a $23 billion water project that the president vetoed in 2007. CNN Capitol Hill producer Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- In an action necessitated by a clerical error in the original bill's passage, Congress on Wednesday enacted a $300 billion farm bill for a second time, overriding President Bush's veto once again.

The Senate voted 80-14 to approve the measure over Bush's objections, following a 317-109 vote in the House of Representatives. Both tallies comfortably exceeded the two-thirds majority required to override the veto, which Bush issued on Wednesday morning.

Congress had overridden an earlier veto of the farm bill last month, despite lawmakers' discovery that 34 pages were missing from the version originally transmitted to the White House.

In rejecting the latest version, Bush objected to its continued subsidies for the wealthy and its reliance on budget gimmicks to conceal a $20 billion increase in spending. Sen. Kent Conrad, chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, countered that the measure would in fact save the government $110 million.

"This bill does not add to the deficit or debt, because this bill is paid for," he said. "That is not my claim. That is the finding of the Congressional Budget Office."

The discovery of the missing section, Title III, prompted concerns among House Republicans that the override vote was improper. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi maintained that the sections of the bill originally sent to the president had become law once Congress voted to override Bush's first veto. To put Title III into effect, however, Congress re-passed the entire legislation—including the omitted pages—and resubmitted it to Bush. The House voted 306-110 at the end of May, and the Senate approved the bill 77-15 in early June.

Two-thirds of the $300 billion in farm bill spending will fund nutrition programs such as food stamps. An additional $40 billion is designated for farm subsidies, while $30 billion is allocated for payments to farms to keep land idle, along with other environmental initiatives.

After vetoing the latest version of the farm bill, Bush admonished Congress on Wednesday for failing to modify "certain objectionable, onerous and fiscally imprudent provisions. ... I am returning this bill for the same reasons as stated in my veto message."

In vetoing the first version, Bush had asserted that the legislation "continues subsidies for the wealthy and increases farm bill spending by more than $20 billion, while using budget gimmicks to hide much of the increase." The president further warned that it would undermine efforts to improve American farmers' access to overseas markets.

Congress has enacted only one other bill over Bush's objections: legislation for a $23 billion water project that the president vetoed in 2007.

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- For a second time on Wednesday, lawmakers moved past President Bush's veto to enact a $300 billion agricultural bill—a repeat action required because of a paperwork mistake made when the legislation first cleared Congress.

The Senate backed the bill 80-14 despite Bush's opposition, coming after the House had approved it by a 317-109 margin. Each of these tallies comfortably exceeded the two-thirds threshold required to reject a presidential veto, which Bush had issued that same Wednesday morning.

Last month, Congress had already voted down a previous veto of the same farm bill, despite lawmakers realizing that 34 pages were absent from the copy first delivered to the White House.

Explaining his rejection of the most recent version, Bush said he opposed the ongoing subsidies going to affluent recipients and the accounting tricks used to conceal a $20 billion boost in expenditures. However, Sen. Kent Conrad, who leads the Senate Budget Committee, countered that the legislation genuinely produces $110 million in savings for the federal government.

"This measure won't grow the deficit or the debt, because it's fully funded," Conrad stated. "That's not just my assertion—it's the conclusion reached by the Congressional Budget Office."

When the absence of Title III came to light, House Republicans raised objections that the override vote might not be legitimate. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi maintained that the portions of the bill first delivered to the president had already become law once Congress voted to reject Bush's initial veto. Nevertheless, in order to enact Title III, lawmakers approved the complete legislation once more—this time including the previously omitted pages—and forwarded it back to Bush. The House cast its 306-110 vote in late May, while the Senate approved the measure 77-15 in early June.

Roughly two-thirds of the bill's $300 billion in funding is designated for nutrition initiatives like food stamps. An additional $40 billion is earmarked for farm subsidies, while $30 billion is set aside for compensating farms that leave land unused as well as for other environmental efforts.

Following his veto of the newest version, Bush criticized Congress on Wednesday for failing to alter "certain objectionable, onerous and fiscally imprudent provisions. ... I am returning this bill for the same reasons as stated in my veto message."

In vetoing the original version, Bush had argued that the bill "continues subsidies for the wealthy and increases farm bill spending by more than $20 billion, while using budget gimmicks to hide much of the increase." He also contended that it would undermine attempts to expand American farmers' entry into foreign markets.

This marks only the second occasion Congress has enacted legislation despite Bush's opposition; the first was a $23 billion water project bill the president rejected in 2007.

CNN Capitol Hill producer Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** -- Congress voted Wednesday to override President Bush's veto of a massive farm bill for the second time, correcting an embarrassing clerical error that had forced lawmakers to redo the entire process.

The unusual situation arose after officials discovered that a 34-page section of the roughly $300 billion bill had been omitted when the legislation was originally sent to the White House. The missing pages meant that the version Bush vetoed—and that Congress subsequently overrode—was technically incomplete, raising questions about whether the law had been properly enacted.

The House voted 317-109 to override the veto, while the Senate followed with an 80-14 vote, both comfortably exceeding the two-thirds majority required to enact the bill over the president's objection.

"This has been an unusual chapter in the legislative process, but the will of Congress is clear," said one Democratic leader following the vote. "American farmers and families who depend on this legislation deserve certainty, and today we've provided it."

The farm bill, which sets agricultural and food policy for the next five years, includes provisions for farm subsidies, nutrition assistance programs including food stamps, and conservation initiatives. The nutrition programs account for the largest share of the spending.

President Bush had vetoed the legislation, criticizing it as bloated and fiscally irresponsible, particularly objecting to subsidies that would flow to wealthy farmers at a time of record crop prices.

"At a time of high food prices and record farm income, this bill lacks the fiscal discipline that Americans expect from their government," the White House said in a statement reiterating the president's opposition.

The clerical error created a rare procedural tangle. Because the enrolled bill sent to the president was missing a section dealing with trade and international food aid programs, congressional lawyers advised that the safest course was to pass the complete legislation again and force another veto and override.

Republicans who opposed the bill seized on the mix-up as evidence of dysfunction. "If we can't even get the paperwork right, how can we trust this Congress to spend $300 billion of taxpayer money wisely?" one GOP lawmaker asked.

Despite the president's objections, the farm bill enjoyed broad bipartisan support, with many Republicans joining Democrats to ensure its passage. Supporters argued the legislation provides critical safety nets for both farmers and low-income families.

# Missing Pages Force Congress to Redo Farm Bill

## A Bureaucratic Blunder Sends Lawmakers Back to the Drawing Board

In one of the more unusual legislative mishaps in recent memory, Congress found itself forced to re-pass the massive 2008 farm bill after discovering that 34 pages had gone missing from the version transmitted to the White House.

## What Happened

The roughly $300 billion Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 had already survived a contentious journey through Capitol Hill. Both the House and Senate had passed the legislation, and lawmakers had even overridden a presidential veto from President George W. Bush, who opposed the bill on grounds that it was too costly and provided subsidies to wealthy farmers.

But shortly after the veto override, officials made a startling discovery: due to a clerical error in the enrollment process, an entire section—Title III, which dealt with international trade and food aid—had been omitted from the version of the bill sent to the White House.

## The Constitutional Complication

The error created a genuine legal problem. Under the Constitution, identical legislation must pass both chambers and be presented to the president in complete form. Because the version Bush had vetoed—and Congress had overridden—was not the full, correct bill, questions arose about whether the entire law, or portions of it, could be considered validly enacted.

The missing Title III wasn't trivial. It authorized food aid programs and international agricultural trade provisions affecting millions of people around the world.

## The Fix

To resolve the ambiguity and ensure the law rested on solid constitutional footing, congressional leaders determined the safest course was to repeat portions of the process. Lawmakers moved to pass the corrected, complete version of the legislation and once again send it to the White House—setting up the possibility of a second veto and a second override.

The episode underscored how even routine administrative functions—like the physical assembly and "enrollment" of a bill's final text—carry significant legal weight in the lawmaking process.

## Why It Mattered

Beyond the embarrassment, the incident highlighted the sheer scale and complexity of modern omnibus legislation. Farm bills routinely stretch to hundreds of pages covering agriculture, nutrition assistance (including food stamps), conservation, and trade. Managing documents of that size across multiple offices and chambers leaves room for human error.

For farmers, food aid recipients, and program administrators awaiting certainty, the delay was an unwelcome complication in an already lengthy political battle. Ultimately, Congress corrected the error and the farm bill became law, but not before providing a memorable lesson in the importance of legislative bookkeeping.

---

*Note: This piece reflects the general circumstances surrounding the 2008 farm bill's enrollment error. For precise procedural details, dates, and vote counts, consult contemporaneous reporting and the official Congressional Record.*

# Bush Vetoes Farm Bill Over Subsidies, Budget Concerns; Conrad Defends Legislation

**WASHINGTON** — President George W. Bush vetoed the sweeping 2008 farm bill this week, citing objections to what he characterized as excessive subsidies flowing to wealthy farmers and criticizing the legislation for relying on budgetary maneuvers that mask its true cost.

The roughly $300 billion measure, which encompasses agricultural subsidies, nutrition assistance, and conservation programs, drew sharp criticism from the White House even as it enjoyed broad bipartisan support in Congress.

## The President's Objections

In rejecting the bill, President Bush argued that the legislation failed to enact meaningful reforms to farm subsidy programs at a time of record agricultural profits and high commodity prices.

"At a time when farm incomes are high, this bill lacks the reform that the American taxpayer deserves," the administration argued, pointing to provisions that would continue directing payments to farmers with substantial incomes.

The White House particularly objected to income eligibility caps that critics said were set too high, allowing individuals earning significant sums to continue collecting government payments. Administration officials contended that subsidies should be targeted toward those who genuinely need support rather than wealthy agricultural operations.

Bush also took aim at what he described as "budget gimmicks" — accounting techniques used to make the bill appear less expensive than its actual long-term cost. The administration argued these maneuvers obscured the true fiscal impact of the legislation.

## Conrad Pushes Back

Senator Kent Conrad, the North Dakota Democrat who chaired the Senate Budget Committee, forcefully defended the legislation and disputed the president's fiscal criticisms.

Conrad, a key architect of the bill, argued that the measure was fiscally responsible and fully paid for. He maintained that the legislation adhered to pay-as-you-go budget rules, meaning new spending was offset rather than added to the deficit.

The senator defended the bill's provisions as essential support for American agriculture and rural communities, emphasizing the importance of programs that provide a safety net for farmers facing volatile markets and uncertain conditions.

Conrad and other supporters noted that the vast majority of the bill's spending was directed toward nutrition programs, including food stamps, rather than farm subsidies — a point they argued the administration's criticism overlooked.

## Congressional Response

The veto set up a confrontation with Congress, where the farm bill had passed with veto-proof majorities in both chambers. Lawmakers from both parties, particularly those representing agricultural states, had strongly backed the measure.

Supporters expressed confidence they had the votes necessary to override the presidential veto and enact the legislation into law despite the White House's objections.

The farm bill, reauthorized roughly every five years, remains one of the most significant pieces of legislation affecting American agriculture, food assistance, and rural policy.

WASHINGTON — Congress moved to override President Bush's veto of a sweeping $290 billion farm bill Wednesday, even as lawmakers grappled with an embarrassing clerical error that left an entire section of the legislation missing from the version sent to the White House.

The five-year measure, which funds farm subsidies, nutrition programs and conservation efforts, cleared both chambers with veto-proof majorities. The House voted 316-108 and the Senate 82-13 to override, well above the two-thirds threshold required in each chamber.

Congressional leaders acknowledged the mistake would require corrective action, potentially forcing lawmakers to repass the full measure and send it back to the White House for a second veto and override.

Republicans seized on the blunder to criticize the Democratic-led Congress, while House and Senate leaders scrambled to determine the proper procedural remedy.

The bill boosted funding for food assistance and expanded eligibility, a provision that drew broad support from anti-hunger advocates and helped secure Democratic backing.

The remaining funds cover farm subsidies, crop insurance and land conservation programs.
